newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian race row MP support grows, govt steady.
newsitem.headline: Australian race row MP support grows, govt steady.

text.p: Australian far-right populist Pauline Hanson's popularity continued to grow steadily as the government's standing marked time, according to a newspaper poll published on Wednesday.
The Sydney Morning Herald poll showed support for Hanson's new One Nation Party increased two points in the past three weeks to 12 percent.
Support for the Liberal-National government and the Labor opposition remained steady at 50-50, after distributing preferences under Australia's complicated voting system.
The latest results rank One Nation, which opposes immigration, Aboriginal welfare and Australia's Asia policy, as the third political power behind the coalition and Labor.
Australia's traditional third force, the Australian Democrats, continued to lose support, dropping to five percent from eight percent.
The government's support before preferences were distributed increased one point to 39 percent and Labor's also rose a point to 35. A month ago, the government's primary vote lead was eight points.
The coalition ended 13 years of Labor rule with a landslide election win in March 1996, with a primary vote of 47.3 percent against Labor's 38.8 percent.

Under Australia's voting system, politicians must win a majority of votes to be elected. To achieve this, ballots for candidates with the lowest support are reallocated according to preferences marked by voters.
The Herald poll found most of Hanson's votes flowing to Labor after preferences.

Prime Minister John Howard's approval rating and support as preferred prime minister over opposition leader Kim Beazley also slipped substantially since the poll last asked those questions, in October 1996.

Howard's approval fell 11 points to 46 percent, while the number of people who disapproved of his performance increased 12 points to 43 percent. Beazley's approval increased four points to 49 percent -- ahead of Howard for the first time -- and his disapproval rating was up two points to 34 percent.
Howard's backing as preferred PM fell to 49 percent from 58 percent and Beazley's increased to 34 percent from 28 percent.
The poll surveyed 2,065 voters around the country by telephone over the last weekend.
